title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–30)
hook: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has a long conversation with Jesus across an old divide

segments.voice: Yesterday, water into wine, John's first semeion, and a mother who said do whatever he tells you. Where did a celebration need your help? Today, more water, and a very long talk. Day fifty-three.

A stranger on a train. A seatmate at a wedding. Sometimes the talk that goes somewhere real is with someone nobody planned to meet. This one happens at a well in Samaria, in the middle of the day. John says it was about the sixth hour: noon, the heat at its worst. Jesus is tired from walking, and he sits down on the edge of the well while his disciples go into town for food. A woman comes out with a jar to draw water. Alone. And he speaks to her. Today, Samaritan.
screen: `A CONVERSATION YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.` → `NOON, AT THE WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES ALONE.`

segments.voice: He says, in the King James Bible: "Give me to drink." And she's startled: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." Jews and Samaritans shared ancestors and the books of Moses, but they had long been divided over where God should be worshiped: Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, right above this well. A Jewish teacher didn't usually ask a Samaritan woman for a drink. He answers: "If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Here's the wordplay. Living water, in Greek and in everyday speech then, meant running water, fresh from a spring, instead of still water in a cistern. She hears the plain meaning: you don't even have a bucket. He means something deeper: water that becomes "a well of water springing up into everlasting life." Then he tells her about her own life: five husbands, and now a man who isn't her husband. Some preachers have assumed she was a scandal, and that's why she came at noon. The text never says why. A woman then could be widowed, or sent away by a husband; John doesn't say what happened. What John does record is a long back-and-forth, about twenty verses of question and answer, and it's with her. She goes back to town, leaving her jar behind, and says: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Orthodox Christians remember her by the name Photini, the enlightened one.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `A JEW ASKS A SAMARITAN.` · `LIVING WATER MEANS RUNNING WATER.` · `SHE LEAVES HER JAR.` · then, large: `A WELL OF WATER SPRINGING UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one person you usually talk to only in passing. Quick hellos, quick texts, logistics. A parent, a coworker, a neighbor, someone who serves you coffee. Picture sitting down with them, no clock, no phone. What might you ask them that you never have? What might they tell you? Let that conversation play out in your mind for a moment. If you pray, you can ask for patience to listen. The bell holds the time.
Samaritan. The woman Jesus meets at the well, from a people long divided from the Jews, whom he still asks, in the heat of noon, for a drink.
Your line: living water. Today, have one unhurried conversation. Put the phone away, ask a real question, and let it run. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: Many churches read the woman at the well during Lent, and Orthodox Christians keep a Sunday of the Samaritan Woman in the Easter season, honoring her as Saint Photini. Christians often read the story when speaking of baptism and of welcoming people across divides.

original.note: Greek: living water. In everyday speech, running water from a spring; in John, a gift that springs up inside.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a woman with a bad reputation.
what it means: a long conversation across a divide, with a woman who then brings her whole town.
what a scholar hears: living water was a pun, running water versus cistern water, and the text never says she was ashamed; that reading came later.

notes: 'One of the longest conversations Jesus has with anyone in the Gospels' — softened from the index hook's 'the longest'; reviewer also softened the hook field to match (meta.index left as the original outline line). Confirm.

Samaritans: shared ancestry and the Pentateuch; worship on Mount Gerizim (John 4:20). A small Samaritan community still exists. Confirm the 'right above this well' description (Jacob's Well near Nablus lies at the foot of Gerizim).
The popular reading that she came at noon to avoid others is marked as not stated in the text; her five husbands are left unexplained.
Photini ('the enlightened one') is her name in Orthodox tradition; Sunday of the Samaritan Woman is the fifth Sunday of Pascha. Confirm.
